transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-22 15:30 UTC | Duration: 45m
Attendees: Alex Chen (AE), Jordan Kim (SE), Priya Rao (CSM) - Redwood; Ellen Rivera (Head of Security), Samir Gupta (VP Eng), Liam O'Connor (SRE), Rina Das (Product) - NimbusBank

Summary:
Quick product walkthrough focused on data handling, retention controls, and redaction features across the API, Console, and Optimize recommendations. Customer is evaluating for payment fraud detection pipelines and has strict PI/PHI retention rules. Interested in a short pilot and verification of SOC2 + KMS integration.

Topics:
- Data retention toggles (request storage on/off)
- Logging redaction and field-level PII masking
- Console UI for retention windows and audit logs
- KMS / HSM integration for encrypted storage
- Performance tradeoffs when request storage is disabled
- Redwood Optimize recommendations for caching vs retention

00:00:05 Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um we wanted to show you the retention flows in the API and also through the console, show how redaction works and then Jordan will run a quick demo with a sample prompt that contains PII.
00:00:18 Ellen Rivera: Great thanks Alex, just to set context, NimbusBank has a strict 30-day retention and some tokens we can't persist at all, we also need full audit logs retained for 7 years but that can be metadata only, not raw request text.
00:00:33 Samir Gupta: And we need to validate KMS integration model for encryption at rest, and ideally ensure no plain text storage of any sensitive fields.
00:00:40 Jordan Kim: Totally, we'll cover both programmatic and console-level controls. Quick note, transcription might have a few flubs, apologies if some product names render slightly off.

00:01:05 Jordan Kim: I'll share my screen — starting with the Console, top-level Data & Security tab. Right here you can see retention policy presets, we have site-default, legal-hold, and ephemeral. Each policy controls request_storage true/false, retention_window days, and audit_log_mode (metadata|full).
00:01:30 Rina Das: When you say request_storage false, does that mean no tokens are persisted at all? Like not even for debugging?
00:01:38 Jordan Kim: Good question — request_storage false disables persistent storage of the raw request and response text. We still log non-sensitive metadata for routing and billing unless you toggle billing metadata off. For debugging we provide an ephemeral session log that expires after 1 hour and is only visible to admins if you enable session debugging.
00:01:58 Liam O'Connor: Is the ephemeral session encrypted with customer KMS or Redwood keys?
00:02:03 Jordan Kim: If you enable Customer-Managed KMS (the VPC/private plan), ephemeral session logs are encrypted with your KMS keys. In hosted scenarios we default to Redwood-managed keys but we support Bring-Your-Own-Key in Dedicated/Private.

00:03:20 Alex Chen: Now switching to the API — you can pass a header x-redwood-retention: off to opt that request out of persistent storage. We also support per-customer default policies on their account so you don't need to set headers everywhere.
00:03:38 Ellen Rivera: Do we get an acknowledgement when a request is marked non-persisted? For compliance we need tamper-evident proof that a request was omitted from storage.
00:03:45 Jordan Kim: Yes — when you flag a request as non-persisted the system emits an audit record with the request_id, timestamp, and policy hash. You can export those audit records to your SIEM via webhook or S3 export. Those audit records do not contain PII or the prompt body.

00:04:10 Samir Gupta: What about redaction rules — can we define field-level redaction or use regex to remove PANs, SSNs, emails?
00:04:18 Jordan Kim: We have multiple layers: 1) pre-processing redaction where you define regex/field templates that strip or mask patterns; 2) post-processing redaction that runs over model outputs; and 3) built-in PII detectors that can flag and optionally scrub entities like emails/SSNs. You can configure these per-route or as account-wide policies.
00:04:44 Ellen Rivera: And are those redaction rules versioned? We need to show change history to auditors.
00:04:50 Jordan Kim: Yes they are versioned — every policy change creates an immutable policy version ID and audit trail. You can also pin policies to a model route so changes don't affect running routes unless you roll forward.

00:05:30 Jordan Kim: I'm going to run a quick live demo — sample prompt contains an account number and email, we'll show request_storage on vs off and redaction rules applied.
00:05:45 Samir Gupta: Heads up, run it against a dummy dataset, don't use actual customer data.
00:05:48 Jordan Kim: Yep using synthetic.

00:06:10 [screen] Jordan Kim: Sending request with request_storage=true, default redaction off. Response shows original email and masked account partly — you can see in the console event log the request text is stored and accessible to admins.
00:06:32 Rina Das: That looks like raw text; can we mask at field-level in the UI?
00:06:37 Jordan Kim: Yep, toggling the route-level redaction to 'mask email' and re-running — now the console shows the masked form and the stored request body is stored already masked.
00:06:52 Ellen Rivera: Ok good. Now show request_storage=false.
00:06:56 Jordan Kim: Switching header x-redwood-retention: off — sending. Response comes back, but console shows 'no stored body' and the audit entry shows request_id + policy hash only. Note: latency increased by ~8ms in this test.
00:07:15 Liam O'Connor: 8ms is fine. What's the percent CPU/memory increase when storage is disabled? Does caching still work?
00:07:22 Jordan Kim: Good question — if request storage is off we can't do prefix caching of exact request text. We still use KV cache for model key/value caches and we have a separate caching layer that can be enabled for non-PII elements. Practically you might see a 5-12% throughput drop in very high QPS workloads if you disable storage and also disable caching. We'll include benchmark numbers in the pilot.

00:08:10 Samir Gupta: Regarding audit logs — you said we can export to S3. Can we set lifecycle policies on that exported data? We need to keep metadata for 7 years but then auto-archive.
00:08:20 Jordan Kim: Yes exports are delivered to your S3 bucket under a path with manifest files; you can apply lifecycle and Glacier transitions on your end. We also offer long-term archive if you'd prefer Redwood to host audit archives under contract.

00:09:05 Ellen Rivera: How do we verify deletion? If we request deletion under GDPR or internal policy, how can we show proof?
00:09:12 Alex Chen: We have a deletion workflow where you submit a deletion ticket via the Console or API; the system produces a signed deletion certificate referencing the request IDs and the storage shards where those records resided. If you have BYOK, the keys are rotated and destroyed for that subset too.

00:10:00 Jordan Kim: Moving to KMS — for Private/Dedicated you can integrate your KMS/HSM and all persisted requests and session artifacts are encrypted with customer keys. The Console shows the KMS connection page and a test vector to validate encryption.
00:10:20 Rina Das: Does Redwood store the plain-text audit manifest anywhere even when BYOK is enabled?
00:10:26 Jordan Kim: The manifest contains only metadata pointers and hashes, no prompt text. Those manifests are encrypted with customer keys when BYOK is enabled.

00:11:15 Samir Gupta: Can we set retention at route-level based on data sensitivity? For example, fraud-analysis routes keep 90 days, onboarding routes 7 days.
00:11:24 Jordan Kim: Absolutely — route-level retention overrides account default. We showed route presets earlier. You can also tag routes and apply policy bundles via the API.

00:12:00 Alex Chen: Quick note on compliance artifacts — SOC2 report, penetration test summaries, and our security whitepaper are in the security docs link I'll share. For contracts we offer privacy addendums and data processing agreements.

00:12:25 Ellen Rivera: We need to validate the legal language specifically around processors and subprocessors.
00:12:30 Alex Chen: We'll have legal send the DPA template; I'll attach the list of subprocessors.

00:13:00 Jordan Kim: Now a short bit on Redwood Optimize — it will analyze token distributions and suggest quantization and caching settings that minimize cost while maintaining your retention constraints. E.g., we can recommend storing only embeddings for certain routes rather than raw text.
00:13:20 Samir Gupta: So Optimize can recommend to store embeddings for analytics and disable request text storage?
00:13:26 Jordan Kim: Exactly. That reduces compliance surface and still gives you ability to run similarity searches.

00:14:10 Rina Das: Are embeddings considered PII? If they are derived from PII, what controls exist?
00:14:18 Jordan Kim: Embeddings can be treated as sensitive; we support marking embeddings as PII and applying tighter retention and audit controls. Also we can salt or one-way transform embeddings on ingest if you need irreversible representations.

00:15:00 [15:00:10] Alex Chen: Quick poll — would you prefer a hosted pilot or Dedicated capacity for the initial tests?
00:15:15 Ellen Rivera: We'd prefer hosted pilot first to validate policy behavior, then move to Dedicated once we sign on.
00:15:22 Samir Gupta: Agreed — hosted pilot as long as BYOK isn't required for initial tests.

00:15:40 Jordan Kim: For the hosted pilot we can enable the retention toggles and BYOK is optional; if you enable BYOK we need a short security review.

00:16:05 Liam O'Connor: One more technical question — if a request is stored but later redaction rules change, do you retroactively scrub old stored data?
00:16:13 Jordan Kim: We support both approaches: immediate re-processing (scrub retroactively) or leave historical data as-is with a versioned policy. You can choose auto-scrub on policy update; this runs as a background job and we provide a scrub log.

00:17:00 Rina Das: What about retention holds for legal matters?
00:17:05 Alex Chen: Legal-hold is a route-level flag that prevents deletion until the hold is removed. Holds create a separate audit entry and the records are exempt from lifecycle deletion.

00:17:45 Samir Gupta: From a performance ops perspective, we need to run nightly benchmarks. Can you provide an automated script to run throughput tests with retention on/off?
00:17:53 Jordan Kim: Yes we'll include a benchmarking script in the pilot repo. It will produce per-token latency and cost numbers.

00:18:30 Ellen Rivera: One more ask: can we get a sample manifest showing the audit webhook payload?
00:18:35 Alex Chen: Absolutely, I'll include sample webhook payloads in the follow-up email.

00:19:10 [small tangential question about pricing] Alex Chen: Pricing-wise, disabling request storage reduces storage fees but may slightly increase per-token inference cost because of reduced caching; Jordan will add approximate delta numbers in the pilot plan.

00:20:00 Jordan Kim: Okay switching to Q&A rapid fire —
00:20:05 Ellen Rivera: Do you certify for PCI?
00:20:09 Alex Chen: We are not PCI-certified as a processor for payment card storage today; we strongly recommend not sending full PANs. We provide redaction tooling and can discuss options for tokenization partners.

00:20:30 Samir Gupta: Any partners for tokenization?
00:20:33 Alex Chen: We can share partner list, and we have integrations with tokenization vendors used by large banks.

00:21:10 Rina Das: For long-term retention of metadata, is there a field-level encryption option?
00:21:16 Jordan Kim: Yes metadata can be encrypted with customer keys and you can restrict access via RBAC down to role-level.

00:22:00 [noise / slight crosstalk]

00:23:05 Jordan Kim: Demo wrap-up — two quick examples: 1) route with request_storage=false + regex redaction + audit webhook; 2) route with request_storage=true + BYOK + audit export to S3 + lifecycle policy. Both are configured via API or Console.
00:23:35 Samir Gupta: Sounds good. We'll test both flows in the pilot.

00:24:00 Alex Chen: Recap & next steps — we'll send SOC2 and whitepaper, Jordan will stand up pilot env with scripts, Samir will provide prompts and success criteria, and we'll schedule the next tech deep dive.
00:24:25 Ellen Rivera: Thanks, appreciate the detail.
00:24:30 Alex Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials.
